blocks.x: Okay, we're here to talk about the New Orleans Jazz Workshop from 1969. I guess we'll start out by maybe talking about just exactly how the workshop started and address kind of the

milieu of what was happening there. Well, the period that the Jazz Workshop developed and... Well, the time that... I mean... Sorry, go ahead. Sorry. The period that we developed the Jazz Workshop was one that was born out of frustration for myself and many of the young jazz musicians during that period of time. And that there were no schools in this immediate area or schools that we knew about to learn more about the techniques of improvisation as far as chord scale relationship. It was pretty much trial and error by going out and sitting in and jam sessions and being out very late hours in clubs and after all places where we would play sometimes after a regular engagement. There were places like Hollies and Birdland and a few other places that would play from, say, 3 to 7 in the morning after Friday night and Saturday night. And this was a traditional thing that happened. But it still was very competitive, but no formal guidelines as far as how to get from point A to B more clearly or more expediently without a lot of hanging out. And the environment was one thing that I thought was not conducive to the development of a young person to be in nightclub or alcohol and other drug-filled environments, which at that particular period of time generally permeated the whole atmosphere.

And prior to that, people like Nat Paralot and Alvin Batiste, Harold Batiste, the American jazz quintet that was Ellis Marsalis and Alvin Batiste and other persons, Chuck Beatty at one time, I think Otis DuVernay. And even earlier than that, I heard people like Ed Blackwell when I was very, very young. But there was no format for younger players to come and learn from those type players. We were searching to develop, if you will, a school of sorts so that a young developing player might get my experience, Alvin Thomas' experience, David Lee's experience, or various different approaches to improvisation so that there would be some sort of chronology as far as what you would tackle or what you would have to work on. And there was also a lack of outlets for modern jazz to be played. It seems like there was almost a hostility in the air for anything post-traditional jazz. The traditional players did not like to call it Dixieland. But that particular type of music was always an inspiration, but it always was reflective of a much earlier period. And I've always felt that the music had a tendency to sound like its particular social times or its particular social settings. So even though I could appreciate the artistry and the musical challenge of some of the traditional music, something about that particular period of time that that music was created was very inharmonious to the 60s, the late 60s, after much of the demonstrations and much of the civil rights movement that was going on. The time called for a music that was much more attuned to where we were moving as a people, not only as black people, but as Americans. I mean, there was a, I felt a harmony that was beginning to develop during mid to late 60s, where all kind of people were coming together celebrating music, celebrating art, and celebrating life in a way that prior to the breakthroughs that the early civil rights movement were just nonexistent in a sense. And my mentor and great person that inspired me so much was John Coltrane. His music was like a healing force during that period of time. And it sort of made you examine yourself and the spiritual and social issues of the time. And it also suggested that we might take music much more seriously than we had up to that point in America. And there were springing up around the country various different workshops and laboratory-type situations where professional jazz musicians were really passing on a tradition and going about it in a very organized, methodical way so that a young person could develop on the instrument much more quickly as far as the theoretical and fundamental harmonic kind of problems that you approach in playing jazz. And just by chance, I happened to play a concert for a lady named Luba Glade, who had an art gallery in the French quarters. And during the intermission, she asked, well, what are some of the things that you really want to do with this music or what do you hope to do in New Orleans? And I mentioned that becoming a little bit tired of playing in the nightclubs, in environments that sometimes the music was really appreciated, but sometimes it's like just a tourist trap and they weren't really that intent on finding out the real depths of the music. Sometimes in a place like the Avent Hall, you'd get serious listeners, and other times you'd get people that would just happen to be there. And we wanted to look for a place where people came to get deeply into this music from a listener's standpoint, from a student's standpoint, and also from a spiritual standpoint. And in my description of what I was hoping for aesthetically, she mentioned that she had a friend named Jules Kahn that had a building on Decatur Street that just might be the perfect venue or might lend itself to just the kind of thing that I had in mind. And secondly, I had no resources. I mean, the financial wherewithal of renting such a facility or owning such a facility. NEA grants and that sort of thing were just becoming popular and widely known during a particular period of time, particularly, I guess, from the things that the Kennedy administration had started. And arts organizations were springing up all over the country. So that was one glimmer of hope. But in meeting with Jules Kahn, he took me to this building that was, I mean, almost the same thing that I had envisioned in my mind's eye in almost a dreamlike state, a place with a little theater in and around, with an open space that might be for a lobby-type area or a gallery-type area in the front or a place where records and refreshments and that sort of thing could be so. And then also this lovely facility upstairs that we hoped to develop later that had what could have been practice rooms and private rooms for teaching and for entertainment and so forth. It had about 20-some rooms on the second and third floor. And I guess it's safe to reveal how much Jules let that building go for now. I mean, it was just something almost unheard of. I mean, to get a three-story building and a French Quarter on Decatur Street. He said, for the first year, you can have this building for $25 a month, which is, I just couldn't believe it. And it needed quite a bit of work. But here again, I feel like it was almost a blessing or divinely or cosmically inspired because one by one, all of the elements and all of the things that I had hoped for or dreamed of were beginning to fall in place. For example, when we finally got the building, we needed a lot of cleanup work and a lot of just physical maintenance and getting it in shape at first and where to get the manpower and how to pay all this manpower and that sort of thing. Well, through some students at Tulane University at that time, and Matt Herron and Eugene Ray, who was a visiting architect and artist that was in residence at Tulane during that time, somehow we got, I don't know, it must have been 40 or 50 kids as volunteers that came from Tulane and came from the community and came in and did the physical labor of hauling trash out, sprucing the place up and then once getting that, getting the walls in condition, spraying the ceiling black, and I mean, everything came together. Paints, supplies were either donated or we played a concert to raise some money to get, say, 20 gallons of black paint to do this. And then I had this aesthetic vision in my mind of how I wanted the room to look. And I thought that it should, first of all, have some focal point as far as central point of universal kind of welcoming atmosphere to welcome all people of all races, of all religions, of all kind of backgrounds. And I think that that was also very closely akin to John Coltrane's influence of really preaching and praying and loving with a cosmic message of people coming together and that the music was like the central or the healing force that would lead us to the creator, to the cosmic. And when Eugene Ray told me that he would design a mural to create this environment in a room, I think that the most that I really expressed was that in the center of the room I'd like to have John Coltrane in the backdrop as the center of the stage, but something that would sort of radiate a glow on and off in the center of the stage. And then I also wanted the star and the crescent, the star of David, the cross, or universal or almost all of the various religious symbols so that a person, Jew or Gentile or Muslim or whomever would feel welcome, felt like this was a place for all people to come. And in the design of his mural, when he first brought the sketches to me, this is, I don't know how to express this other than when I saw the sketches, not only was it something that I had not told him other than those basic things, when I saw the sketches, the design, the way it fit the curvature of the room and the way it brought the whole room into one mind and made the center of the stage and the musicians and all, it seemed like the whole center of concentration for the whole audience was focused toward center and focused toward train and then focused out into these various symbols. But his drawings and his rendition, even though it's down to scale, looked exactly what I had been seeing in my dreams and in my mind's eye. It was almost a photograph of my thoughts. And the more these particular type things started happening, I knew that something very special was about to happen in the development of that, I don't guess we can call it a club. I often thought of the jazz workshop as being a school,

but more like a temple or a place to come and bathe yourself in music and to pray in music. And when we did play in that room, not only were the musicians very telepathic, but many, many times, and as a listener, if you were there, I'm sure you may have experienced the same thing, where sometimes we would be transported to a zone where it felt like the whole room was of one mind and the music was happening right there. Because a great majority of what we played was happening on the spot, even though it might have been a conventional composition or a standard tune, we would go to new and fresh places almost every time we played. But it sounded like something that we might have worked on for months and months and months to get together. And the people just seemed like they would travel with us. And I remember many times just being lost in sound and lost in space and lost in this embrace of people. I've never had musical experiences quite like that any other time in my life. I've had very profound experiences that happened, but that particular room had some very, very special things happening in it. And in the development of the concepts that I'm talking about, we saw that photography and all of the other arts were... Excuse me.
Can we get that out there, Brad?
Yeah, that's no problem.

Okay. We saw that photography and the other aspects of art could also be brought into that same kind of setting or to bring about a unity, a integration of music and photography, music and painting, the way the mural expressed it. The mural that Eugene Ray designed, for example, was singing all the time or playing all the time. And it was something that was done, but it seemed to fit the mood and the moment or the magic of everything that was happening.

And another amazing aspect of what happened with that is that Eugene had done this drawing on scale size, I mean drawing down a scale, and then he had measurements of how big this was supposed to be on this wall and how big this was supposed to be here and what colors were supposed to happen here. And they were very vivid at that time what we called day glow paints or things that were illuminated more so by black light or the purplish type of ultraviolet light that you see. And he brought in art students and architecture students from Tulane. And here again they took this thing and they traced this mural throughout the room and came in at different shifts. I mean it must have been for months of painting and bringing this thing into reality. But there also was a lady named Mona McMurray who was like a, I guess a magical mother or fairy godmother in a sense. I mean it looked like all the little things that you could think of that we didn't know how to get our hands on. Stage lighting and she had some old stage lights. She knew a friend that had these type of props. She knew somebody that had this to make this sound booth work together. And then there was a man named Gary Edwards who later had a musical supply house here. But we couldn't put together the kind of sound system that we needed. And at first he said, well I'll loan you one until you can get it together. And he said, no, I'll give you one. He designed a sound system for that room. And there was some speakers and all in the control booth set up the whole thing. There were some people here named, I think it was Carol and James Burns who connected with the museum. And there was a grand piano that was in very, very bad shape but that was of no use to them. That we could have gotten some work done to. Here came a grand piano for us to have in the jazz workshop. All of the various elements of things that were absolutely vital and essential to setting up a foundation to have this room vibrant and happening came together primarily through volunteers from every kind of walk of life. And Decatur Street at that time was, well it was the back of the French market in that particular section. There were a lot of derelicts and skid row type people all permeating through the whole area. And that particular end of Decatur Street was not even thought of as far as nightclubs or entertainment sort of thing. It was somewhat projected that they were going to do this renovation in the next couple of blocks next to Morning Call where Al Hurt later had a place that was developed there. But at the time that we were in the jazz workshop it was like no vision or no way could this happen. I think that that might have been part of the catalyst to people seeing some hope there. But the people that were really devout to the music, they didn't mind coming into the area. They didn't mind coming into contact with all the things that they would have to face en route to the jazz workshop. Because once you got in that door, once you got in, you knew that all the trouble you had taken to get there was worth it to get there. And also it welcomed you. And anybody that was, let's say, of a negative vibratory rate or not attuned to that music or not attuned to the love that was in that room, it seems like when they would walk in, they would hurry up and run out of there. This is the wrong place for me. These people are too unified or whatever. But it was a warm environment like that. And we had all kinds of people, a lot of college students, a lot of arts patrons that were just very curious because they knew that something new and something exciting was happening here. Also, we were playing a music at that time that we played some spontaneous improvisation or spontaneous compositions during that particular period of time. Willie T, who's my brother, George Davis and David Lee and myself, we would play together every day. We had been doing this for a couple of years at that point. Just about noon after getting up from a night, we'd work till like maybe 1, 2, 3 o'clock in the morning, get a good somewhat of a night's sleep. And around 11, 30, 12 o'clock, we would get together every day predominantly in George Davis' garage. We had a little small tape recorder, but we would just go in and play. Sometimes we would rehearse a specific tune, but oftentimes we would just tune into each other and just start playing. And sometimes this would go on for an hour, hour and a half, two hours. And we would segue from, say, maybe an original composition to something like Stella by Starlight or all the things you are. And then we'd go into some free or collective improvisation. But we were trying to include as many of the elements of standard jazz playing, rhythm changes, the blues. And at that time, I mean, like the Coltrane things that would be just becoming, which are standards now, I mean, things like Giant Steps, Moments Notice, all those kind of things. We were working on that kind of material and trying to learn how to play the standard repertoire. But we were also trying to incorporate some of these freer elements that was in some of Train's later music and Ornette Coleman's music. I mean, all of these influences were coming in. And the one thing that we tried to avoid was playing anybody else's statements or anything that they played. We tried to avoid playing anybody else's stuff verbatim. We might have played any like manner or like Ornette-ish or like the great group that Miles had during the late 60s with Tony and Ron and Herbie. And the magic that was happening in those rhythm sections. We were inspired by those things, but also trying to approach it from our own unique, intuitive kind of interpretation. That unless there was a real problem with what was happening musically, we tried to put it down on tape and just let it happen automatically or intuitively. And then go back and listen to the tapes and see what of this body of work we had just completed that we really liked, what we didn't like, what we wanted to keep. And when we recognized something that was very distinctly an element that we thought was unique and not like anybody else's stuff, then we would make a comment, well, we should include that in our playing from time to time. And when we do that, certain things we began to recognize. And the other thing that I'm more keenly aware of now is that we were playing some things that were so fresh and so new. This is some of the things that later Cannonball Adley would come in to record and also to talk about is that we were playing some new music that was unlike anything that I had heard other people play. And it was distinctively our music as well as when we wanted to play things that were of a common genre or that were popular in a jazz context that you knew that we were playing a train tune or that we were playing a Cannonball Adley tune or a Savonu tune or an Ornette tune. And the things that we were playing, the things that we were playing, we had not analyzed or no one had really analyzed. And we were awfully concerned, well, how do we explain what we're doing to someone else? And my brother, who's always had the, I mean, he's one of the most prolific composers I've ever met, but he does not directly read or write. He does not directly read or write. And stuff like pass this on or how to teach other young players to play that particular idiom or play those kind of things. And the period that we were putting this music together was also after, I mean, in my late high school years, say like 58, 59, going into 60, that was a very, there were some very vibrant things happening with Nat Parallot and Ellis and all those persons. And then during the very mid-60s, it seemed like most of those persons were either away and there was no real vibrant modern jazz stuff happening for a few years. I think Ellis might have been with Al Hurt during a particular period that we became very active, but those concerts that used to happen all the time were not happening so much then. And we said something has to be done to keep this alive and keep this, be at the forefront of creating some new New Orleans music to make not only ourselves constantly grow, but to inspire younger musicians to come up. Because I remember walking out River Road many, many nights from my parents' home on Monroe Street down to Oak Street and all the way out River Road to where Ellis had taken his home and transformed that into a place called the Music Haven. And it was like a very dreamlike jazz club. I mean, it was like my ideal kind of jazz club. He had his grand piano there, but he had taken what had been his house or his home and converted it into a place that was aesthetic as far as a room with good acoustics. James Black, Marshall Smith, Nat Parallot and Ellis. It was like going into a time warp. But when you consider what you encountered in all the other jazz settings or little places that were about, when you went there, you could just be suspended in a place where it was just heard nothing but wonderful music for two, three, four hours at a time. And that was an inspiration to me. But after that, there was a void, a period where there was very little happening for a while. And the closest thing that came to that was when Gloria De Freitas opened Gloria's jazz room on Roman in Spain that we played in, must have been about 65, 66, 67, like during that period. And then when that sort of faded out, I mean, she paid us extremely well, had all of the things that we needed. But yet again, it was in an alcohol environment or other things happening in and around clubs. And I was very inspired by Preservation Hall, which had, or it was another place on Bourbon Street. I think they might have called it Economy Hall or something during that time. But the thing about it was that no drinks. There were not drugs on the premises or it was just pure come in to hear the music, nothing elaborate. The thing that you came there to hear was the music. That's what you came for. And then afterwards, you went out for whatever libation or whatever kind of indulgences you wanted to do before or after. But when you came to that place, you came to hear just the music and the other things associated to the music. So I wanted to see an environment similar to that for the new music or for what I was terming during that particular time, the new New Orleans music or new New Orleans jazz. And to make an emphasis that whereas they were stressing preservation, we wanted to stress the evolution of the music. Because at one point we started to call it Evolution Hall or rather than a jazz workshop. But, you know...

if you're involved in the evolution of a music, then naturally you would have to go back and study the music from its inception or from its very beginning and find out what all the masters that came before, so that you would have a chronological insight, a chronological appreciation from a student's standpoint to know the lineage of the drummers, the lineage of the soprano, saxophone players, clarinetists, and so on through all the instruments, and to see how what we were playing at that time, which was often thought of as being rather avant-garde, and we were playing sometimes tonally, but at the other aspect we were playing changes and we were playing conventional chord changes and conventional tunes. We'd take, I remember April, and we were always playing the right changes at the right time, but we would take it some other places, and David Lee was playing other kind of stuff, metrically, because you would hear David play and think that you were hearing two or three drummers because he could play and imply one thing and have something else going on with the bass drum, but it was so contrapuntal or multi-metric, but the basic pulse would always be there. I mean there was really some really exciting things happening, and there was some resistance to it, but the musicians were just always, I mean they were just blown away every time they came to hear us play. And whereas Ellis and the guys that we learned, that I learned from Alvin Batiste, who's my teacher during that time, could explain quite a bit of the fundamentals of what it took to develop this music. Other than the most conventional approaches, there was much about what we were doing, that needed time for us to take and play or tape and analyze and find out what was happening so that we can pass. Most of the musicians that were developing, or persons of our peers, would say, what are you doing? What's that you're playing? How do you all get that particular effect, or what kind of changes are you playing? What are you playing there? Other than tunes like that we were playing, maybe I remember April tune up other familiar jazz standards, but when we started playing this music that was particularly the collective music of David, George, Willie and myself, Cannonball Adderley and some other people that had come down from New York recognized it and said, man this is some fresh stuff. I've not heard anybody playing the way that you play, especially the way you play, and you cover so many different idioms, but it also has a purity in what's happening. They could hear the blues, they could hear us when we played directly on a particular set of changes, or the unorthodox way that some of the changes to some of Willie's tunes were happening. People wanted to know what this was or what we were doing because they could hear it was something fresh, and we knew that it had to be, in addition to performing for the people on a nightly basis, a place where we could come and experiment and explore and examine this music. And a couple of Porgy Jones used to come by, Fred Kemp used to come by, a lot of the players that you see currently on the scene now, but I think one of the persons that sticks in my mind that I remember most vividly than almost anybody else was John Vodakovich, who was maybe, if not a freshman, very early in his development, about to go to Loyola or at Loyola, but he was playing at the Playboy Club with Al Baleta every night. And he would bring other musicians over with him to come, so you got to come over here and hear what these guys are doing. And almost on a nightly basis, when they were off, or as soon as they got off from their club gigs, there was a trumpet player named Warren Looning that he brought by one time, or Jay Cave, who's a bass player who's now in Las Vegas. I mean, all of these musicians that wanted to play some fresh and new music and that wanted to play also from a bebop tradition and on would come by. But John was there because David was playing something that that was just absolutely fascinating. I think of, I liked some of what I was playing that during that particular period of time, but I was also searching and exploring. But David was playing something that was just knocking everybody out. I mean, he was playing things that when Roy McCurdy would come in town with Cannonball. Even the most advanced trummers that you'd heard name people when they came to town to come and hear us play, or sometimes Cannonball would come over with the group after they finished the set at Al Hurts or something. And they would come in and listen to this music and encourage us and say, man, you got to take this group to New York or you have to be recorded because something's happening here that other people need to hear. And as an offshoot of that, what we did, since we had no particular funding during that particular time and we had no grants or anything of that sort, we just decided that until we did, we would go around and get music students from various different schools and invite them to come out to the workshop or come out on a Saturday afternoon. And many times we would just go into areas where we knew there were kids that wanted to learn and go and pick them up in our car or pick them up in George's car on somebody's station wagon and just get a group of kids into the workshop and play for them. And then one by one, have them come up and play with the rhythm section of let a drummer sit in after listening to David for a while. And that was the intent to develop a place where we could structure some things. uh, and design some classes, uh, because jazz education was like, uh, not particularly happening in New Orleans at, at that time, uh, as far as a school, a formal type of type of structure. And we wanted to see to, to that there was some place where musicians would not have to, especially young players would not have to go out and wonder what was happening and sit out and, and, and go to, go to clubs and just sit and struggle through things, but somewhere where you could take it step by step going from the blues into rhythm changes and gradually into more complicated type changes. And, uh, George Davis was very advanced harmonically. He knew a lot. Uh, in addition to wanting to teach each other, we had, we took time of, um, constructive criticism. If George played something I particularly liked, uh, that I didn't like, um, I would point out certain things that if, if there were incorrect approaches that were, that I was using on something, he would take time and explain it to me theoretically. I'll try this. I'll try this particular kind of scale on this, this particular group of chords or something and see how that works. So there was that kind of experimentation going on and people like, uh, with Kemp would be, uh, Fred Shepard and, uh, just a group of, I mean, Alvin Thomas, Clyde Kerr, all of those guys would drop in at different times or come in and sit in or we just talk music. Um, but from a more, let's tear it apart. Let's see what's happening. What's happening. So whenever we could, uh, meet after a gig or if we happen to be uptown at, uh, there's a place called, uh, Dorothy's, uh, steakhouse, which later became Leroy's on LaSalle Street where all the musicians would gather, uh, later on, instead of meeting there, sometimes they would all come down to the workshop and jam. And many times after the night was over and the people were gone from the club, we would just lock the doors. I remember nights of playing in there until four or five, six o'clock in the morning with the doors locked, just playing and playing away. I remember, um, Cecil Bridgewater, who's now playing with, uh, Max Roach, uh, coming in one time, he was, I think he was at, uh, Illinois State or one of the schools out of, out of, uh, Chicago that would, that had a jazz program. And that whole big band came down one time for a festival or some, for some performances. And we had Cecil and a lot of the players, uh, that would, that would pretty much our peers then, like they were, they were in their early twenties. Um, some of them still teenagers, really exploring and developing music. And whenever we could get, uh, groups like that in, they would come in and have these jam sessions that would go on and on through the night or by word of mouth, um, cannonball would pass on to, to somebody or other bands that had come through and heard this. When musicians were coming to this area, we would get phone calls that were coming down to New Orleans for a couple of days. We heard about your workshop. We want to see what we can do with, uh, when we come in, can we come over and play some or just find out what was possible. And, uh, uh, Joe's Avenue spent a lot of time with my brother because, um, he had very, very advanced technique and theoretical understanding, but Willie was doing some things that were like, we always said, it feels good and sounds good, but it's very unconventional to, to some of the other things that were happening. So he wanted to find out what was this stuff that he was, he was playing. Um, I'm trying to, there was a, um, a young woman, I can't place the last name right now, but Angie was an organ player. Um, that was just fascinating. I think she was, uh, Romanian, uh, used to play in some clubs here at one particular period of time. She brought a group of, uh, European students that, that she knew that were jazz students over. It was just a whole conglomeration of, of, of people that were exploring the music and trying to find out what was happening with the music. And then there was a period that after word of mouth started getting out about what we were doing with the jazz workshop, um, there's a man named Charles Sua, who was with the, uh, Orleans Parish School Board. And at that time, Shirley Trustee was working closely with him. And they were fascinated with our idea of developing a jazz curriculum or developing a school for the arts in a sense. So many times we would go down to the school board office and have these sessions, which should have been consultation really, uh, of how we thought a school for the arts should have been designed or what, what the curriculum should have been for jazz students and so forth. And, uh, one project that developed out of that was to take, uh, David Lee and, uh, Willie, George Davis, and what was, what might sound like a strange combination was the same group that we had that was called Willie Tina souls with the addition of Alvin Alcorn, who's Sam Alcorn's father, who was a very, very, uh, great trumpet player that was also one of Louis Armstrong's favorite players. And we were the one of, one of the main things we were trying to try to show was that even though he played in an idiom that was so-called traditional, that the things that we were playing were so akin to so, so alike that we could take a player from that particular generation, uh, and the things that George and David were playing and the newer things that Willie was playing and combine these musics and come up with a music that really was one music because I've never looked at this music as being, uh, really as separated as the record companies or musicologists try to separate, but I look at it as something that's ongoing and constantly developing. And if you have the basic elements there, uh, that's a lot of the poetry from the Harlem Renaissance, uh, Gwendolyn Brooks and, uh, Langston Hughes, uh, some other poets. And we proceeded to record some spontaneous improvisation to these, to this poetry as well as some preset type of things that we did to, to, to the poetry. And this was a project that was designed to be played in junior and senior high schools in the public school system. So, um, this was the seed, like, like a seed or a germ of an idea, um, that really was, uh, something that would begin to introduce jazz into the public school and also uh, uh, a germ of a seed of an idea of developing what later became, uh, NOCA. Uh, cause our suggestion at that time was that there should be an instructor in all the various different disciplines of genre, uh, art teachers, drama teachers, music teachers, uh, photography, like we had with the Listening Eye Gallery that Matt Heron and Mike Smith and a lot, uh, a lot of the photographers were developing in the front part of the building, that all of these things were, were things that should come together and that should be happening in the School for the Arts. Um, so you had a broad base of interest and a broad base of people from all kind of walks coming together to try to see what would happen in this, in this, uh, in this building that we had hopes of becoming a great institution. And for, for its particular duration and for its particular life, it was like a very vibrant, uh, it gave a, a wake up or, uh, stuff like stuff stuff like

Okay. How do you want the workshop remembered?

I want the workshop remembered as a place for people to become cognizant of just the kind of sacrifice and dedication that musicians and all artists put into their work, uh, so that they can bring a part of themselves and a part of their experience in sharing themselves with people. Uh, to be remembered as a place that some of new, the seeds and the foundation of some of the greatest New Orleans music that you hear now and that you've heard in the past few years that what we at the workshop and all of those volunteers and all those people that came together to make happen, uh, what kind of impact that had on what you're hearing now and without it, I don't think we, we would have quite as rich of a musical environment as we have as a result of what, what we put into that workshop and, uh, hopefully something that will make the, the people that turn the wheels that operate the, the city and all its various institutions to recognize that never again can we allow ourselves to be negligent of not reaching out and developing all of the fresh talents that are in its raw and formative stages to try to do everything we can to give them the right guidance, the right instructors, and the right environment to develop in and hopefully that we, we know that, uh, the music is, is a very serious art form, it's, uh, America's greatest art form in, in my evaluation and many, many others of, of the giants and masters that I've met. I think it's no doubt that, uh, jazz music has gone on to impact and influence all of the world and when we know that it came from here, uh, as one of my earliest music teachers told me, most people have to go to New York or go to here and, and,

to explore some of these things. But when you come from New Orleans, you're a branch off the original tree. This is where it started. So it's like being a direct descendant of Sidney Bechet or Louis Cottrell or Willie Humphrey and on and on and on the great people that came afterwards. I learned from Alvin Baptiste and Wes Anderson learned from Alvin Baptiste and I taught Wes. And we all somehow wind up teaching each other either something of music or a life of spirituality or just sharing our lives together. Those roots go very, very deep and we're all entangled and entwined and all for positive, forceful good. I mean, I don't think that there's... Anytime I see any one of us in the musical community that we have here make great strides or from collaborations that I've had or things that they've passed on, I'm always happy to see the other successes that come. And I'm just happy that myself and David and all the rest of us have had a chance to put our hearts and souls into some projects and to see that it's an ongoing music and I know that it will never fade out or die because you see all these new things that's happening. One of the other things I always thought about the workshop is that to play the kind of music that the extended forms of jazz or from bebop and beyond or the newer music, you need great technical facility and I would also hope that some of the young musicians that we see that have tremendous talent that are somewhat playing raw on the streets and not getting the very direct private lessons and musical lessons that allow them to take their talents even further that we sort of develop this raw talent that we see playing on the streets and somehow form a workshop or places that they can go to not only play the music they play but get individual development and instruction and compositional guidance, theoretical guidance so that they can be the very best that they can be.
Okay. Was that Clyde Kerr Sr. who said that to you? Who was your teacher who said that you came?
Willie Humphrey.
Willie Humphrey.

Willie Humphrey, who's still alive and I think in his 80s now one of the great clarinet players. He and his brother Percy play down at Preservation Hall but Willie Humphrey I met through a scholarship I used to play on the radio every Sunday afternoon when I was in junior high school on a Peter Champ Clark show that was called Stars of Tomorrow and at that time my influences were Earl Bostic and Louis Jordan and I liked Sam Butera during that time and I remember him making a comment one time when I was playing saying who knows maybe he'll be another Charlie Parker and I was about 12, 13 years old and I said Charlie Parker, who's that? because I wasn't quite I didn't become aware of Bird until like a little later on like just as I was about to enter high school and I really knew what he meant and from that radio show I won a scholarship to Educational Gateways and Willie Humphrey happened to be my clarinet teacher but of Clyde Kerr Sr. there's not enough that can be said about him I think maybe a good 70, 75% of all of the good musicians that you hear playing now at some point came through him the man made a he consecrated his life to teaching and passing on and writing music now that's an institution that really needs some exploration because he and Alvin Batiste I often say are probably the two most profound music teachers that I've ever had not only because of what they gave me musically but they gave so much of them stuff

segments.title: Why the Jazz Workshop began: no schools, only clubs and jam sessions
segments.summary: Turbinton says the 1969 workshop grew out of young musicians' frustration at having no place to learn improvisation, only late-night jam sessions in drug-and-alcohol clubs.

segments.title: Mentors, Coltrane, and finding the Decatur Street building
segments.summary: He recalls earlier modern players, Coltrane's spiritual influence, the lack of outlets for modern jazz, and how Luba Glade and Jules Kahn led him to a cheap three-story Decatur Street building, volunteers and Eugene Ray's Coltrane mural.

segments.title: The workshop as a temple: telepathic playing and the arts together
segments.summary: He describes the room as a place to pray in music, with collective improvisation and a sense of one mind, and the plan to join photography and painting with music.

segments.title: Volunteers, donated equipment, and the daily quartet rehearsals
segments.summary: Volunteers supplied lights, a sound system and a piano; Decatur Street was then skid row. He explains how he, Willie T, George Davis and David Lee rehearsed daily, taping free and standard material, and their earlier New Orleans scene.

segments.title: Visiting musicians, teaching kids, and the school-board jazz curriculum project
segments.summary: Cannonball Adderley and local players came to hear the group, kids were brought in to sit in, and the school board backed a project pairing the quartet with Alvin Alcorn and poetry as a seed for NOCA.

segments.title: Keeping the Workshop going: money, sacrifice, and young players it inspired
segments.summary: He covers doing everything from janitor to door collection, shrinking pay, selling his car, volunteer Quint Davis, and later results such as Terence Blanchard sitting in.

segments.title: Pause in recording
segments.summary: A short break and chatter about a reverb chamber in the room.

segments.title: The Workshop's audience, Decatur Street hippies, and admission policy
segments.summary: He describes patrons, hippies and wealthy uptowners sharing the room, the racial mixing, and the concert-style rule of no food or drink with a $2 door.

segments.title: Free Southern Theater, donated instruments, fundraising and the opening
segments.summary: John O'Neal and the Free Southern Theater gave funding advice, instruments were collected for poor kids, a fundraising party and the fire code work followed, and the Workshop opened and then slid into debt as Dizzy hired George and David.

segments.title: Closing the Workshop and what the quartet members did next
segments.summary: He recalls padlocking the building, then taking tapes to New York, recording with Zawinul, touring with B.B. King, and the quartet's members scattering without ever reuniting.

segments.title: Why the Workshop closed: economics and the need for arts education
segments.summary: He blames economics, noting the group's earnings and the absence of mentors, and argues New Orleans needed jazz and arts education.

segments.title: The Workshop's fruit: John Vodakovich on drums and the group Trinity
segments.summary: Without David Lee he struggled to find a drummer and used John Vodakovich, despite criticism, later playing with David Lee and James Singleton in Trinity.

segments.title: How he wants the Workshop remembered
segments.summary: He wants it remembered for artists' sacrifice and as a seed of current New Orleans music, urging the city to nurture young talent.

segments.title: New Orleans roots, teaching lineage, and a workshop for street players
segments.summary: He says New Orleans musicians descend from the originators, names the teacher lineage through Alvin Batiste to Wes Anderson, and hopes for a workshop for raw young talent.

segments.title: Willie Humphrey, Educational Gateways, and Clyde Kerr Sr. as teachers
segments.summary: He identifies Willie Humphrey as his clarinet teacher, won through a Sunday radio show scholarship at about age 12-13, and praises Clyde Kerr Sr. as a major teacher.
